newsitem.title: USA: U.S. agencies propose new Columbia Basin land plan.
newsitem.headline: U.S. agencies propose new Columbia Basin land plan.

text.p: The Clinton administration Wednesday proposed a sweeping plan for managing more than 72 million acres of land in the Northwest that environmental groups, loggers, ranchers and miners have long fought to control.

The controversial plan, endorsed by several U.S. agencies, called for more forest thinning and controlled forest burns to protect old growth trees from wildfires, and more watershed protections in two areas covering the Columbia, Klamath and Great Basins.
It was put together after a broad scientific study of the region showed that land, water and salmon populations in the area were in desperate need of restoration.
"We have a landscape that is out of sync, out of balance and in poor health," William Stelle, regional director of the National Marine Fisheries Service, said at a news briefing.

The proposal was meant to spur land managers to coordinate their approaches to protect forests, lakes and rivers, and revive salmon and wildlife populations, without giving specific rules to block land use or development.
Officials from several agencies, led by the Bureau of Land Management and the Forest Service, expect to revise the plan over the next year after a four-month public comment period.

Regional Forester Robert Williams of the Forest Service said his agency was concerned the strategy for preserving old growth trees would cut into timber sales, which in turn would limit the revenue the agency needed to carry out its environmental plan.
"We expect we will have more low value sales," he said.
He said ideally the agency would like to do two to three times the amount of prescribed fires that it is doing now, if it can obtain the funding from Congress.
But loggers said the forest thinning and burn plan would not work.

"The trees are so small, with the species composition they're proposing very few people are going to be able to bid on these sales," said Chris West, vice president of the Northwest Forestry Association. "As a result, they're not going to be able to meet their goals ... for restoration."
Environmental groups were concerned that the plan failed to protect undeveloped forests, which had the richest range of species.
